extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR writers, communicators, and campaign strategists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing public relations materials—especially news releases—and for evaluating promotional campaigns and PR writing for accuracy, impact, and long-term consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure multiple campaign objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional campaigns should be evaluated on the full set of communication objectives (communication, retention of the message, acceptance of cognitions, formation/change of attitude, and overt behavior), not only on behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s important to measure behavior, but measures of behavior alone may make a campaign appear to fail when it has been successful for a particular public. Use the objectives discussed throughout the book; measures for these objectives can be taken from the samples in Chapter 9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include coorientational effects in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: As promotional campaigns become symmetric as well as asymmetric, evaluate the coorientational version of effects (how publics and the organization align or misalign in perceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When campaigns are symmetric/asymmetric, measure coorientational effects described in Chapter 6; include these alongside the other communication objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic writing objectives—aim primarily for message retention
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing, use the five communication effects as objectives, but recognize that writing most reliably produces message retention; writing alone rarely guarantees exposure, acceptance, attitude change, or overt behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the five effects (communication, retention, acceptance of cognitions, formation/change of attitude, overt behavior) in mind. Because writers cannot control exposure or readers’ beliefs, strive primarily for clarity and retention; other effects require additional strategies beyond writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: PR writing should aim to be as objective as possible—giving facts so readers can decide—by avoiding self-serving puffery and personal-value phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the writer out of the story (avoid I/subjective adjectives), present observable details rather than judgments, and ensure anonymous PR copy carries self-evident authority and integrity so readers will accept it despite lack of a byline. Balance loyalty to the employer (gathering info there) with the editor/reader’s needs when assembling the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puffery and self-serving language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use gratuitous promotional phrases (e.g., 'public-spirited gesture,' 'generous gift,' sentimental image sentences) in news releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors resent blatant, self-serving phrases; puffery may cause a release to be ignored. Write straight, factual leads that editors can use without heavy editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source review and factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practice commonly involves source review of copy prior to publication to improve factual accuracy and avoid embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike journalists (who usually do not allow source prepublication review), PR writers should have knowledgeable sources check facts and quotes. The PR practitioner must also be able to accept technical corrections from supervisors and incorporate them while preserving style and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider long-range implications and message consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: PR writing must consider how messages cumulatively position the organization over time; consistency and repetition help maintain or reposition organizational image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review past articles to see how the public perceives the organization; adopt consistent phraseology (e.g., agreed institutional descriptors) and repeat core messages for passive audiences to implant recognition and maintain 'market position' in the marketplace of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition for passive publics
rubrics_metrics.description: When analysis shows publics will process messages passively, repetition is necessary for retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat the message over time so passive receivers will at least retain some of it; choose concise expressions and use them faithfully across communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity versus completeness (provide both)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the news system favors simplification, provide a concise, easily digestible press release for immediate use, and supply more complete background (press packet, fact sheets) for in-depth reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a succinct, readable release (example: a 12-paragraph release) while distributing a press packet with fact sheets or arranging experts at a news conference to supply depth. This lets media use the short version or pursue the long version as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and write for reader relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by identifying and identifying with readers; make the story relevant by explaining what's in it for them and tying the story to readers' involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring the story 'close to home'—focus on effects for consumers or communities rather than organizational announcements. If involvement is low, compensate by simplifying and brightening the writing to arouse curiosity or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize the story—use people and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanize content by including people’s reactions and short memorable quotes from those affected by the program or product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes that are brief and memorable; synthesize broader comments into one or two sentences that illustrate impact and help retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise style — short words, sentences, and paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Write short words, short sentences, and short paragraphs to make messages digestible and to suit the media’s simplification process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep sentences and paragraphs brief; use an occasional longer sentence for variety. Packaging information in bite-sized pieces makes it more palatable for low-involvement audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud and use punctuation for 'visual relief'
rubrics_metrics.description: Read copy aloud and add punctuation where natural breaks or explanatory phrases occur to help the reader’s eye and oral comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuate to indicate pauses and explanatory inserts; this visual relief supplements structural punctuation and aids readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcapitalization and follow news style
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid capitalizing every subcommittee or program; adhere to news-style capitalization and usage (e.g., Associated Press style) to match media expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitals only for proper names and full organizations (e.g., 'Consolidated Edison' but 'Con Ed’s rate advisory board'). Following AP style enhances an editor’s willingness to use your release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and format to the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulate straight news style for basic releases, feature style for magazine articles, and conversational tone for speeches or scripts; PR writing should blend into the medium so the audience doesn’t identify it as 'PR.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the expected style for each medium and shift tone accordingly; the best PR writing adopts the medium’s voice so readers/listeners accept the message naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate writing objectively and iteratively
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing can and should be evaluated: put copy aside and re-read after a few days, ask others to paraphrase your message, and use formal readability tests and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readability tests (see Chapter 9) and the Signaled Stopping Technique (SST): have readers indicate where they want to stop and why (confusion, rereading, disagreement). Use feedback to rewrite—'Good writing is not merely written... it is rewritten.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criteria — when to issue a press release
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue news releases for items that are genuinely newsworthy to target media/audiences, such as management appointments, advertising agency changes, new product introductions, milestones, cost savings or conservation programs, and significant local/regional developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which media will find the item newsworthy (community weeklies, trade journals, regional magazines) and tailor the release accordingly; list examples—milestones, new savings/economies, plant modernization, management changes—to guide selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide supporting materials for depth (press packet/fact sheets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accompany concise releases with press packets or fact sheets that develop specifics for reporters who need more detail for in-depth stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the press packet as background for features or magazine pieces and ensure experts are available at news conferences to answer probing questions; this preserves the concise release while enabling fuller coverage.
